title: Generics: why they arrived and what problem they solve

videos.script: Lesson 29 asked an interface value what it was holding, while the program ran. This lesson is about not having to ask. {{twice}} It starts with one function written twice. A sum for ints and a sum for floats: the same seven lines, with different types. {{workarounds}} Before type parameters, Go had three ways around that. Copy the function. Take any, and check the type at run time. Or ask for methods, through an interface. The standard library's sort package still carries all three. {{sum}} Then the fourth way. One Sum, with a type parameter in square brackets. The compiler checks every call, so a wrong type never reaches a running program. {{library}} You have used functions like this for a while already. The slices and maps packages are made of them. {{when}} Last, when not to bother. A type parameter that only ever stands for one type is a cost with nothing in return. By the end you can tell which of the four ways a piece of Go is using, and why it was chosen.
